title: How To Improve Listening With Strategic Pausing https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2017/01/14/how-to-improve-listening-with-strategic-pausing/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin addresses the common frustration of feeling like students aren't truly listening, tracing much of the problem to teachers speaking too quickly without realizing it. He outlines three strategic pausing techniques: pausing briefly between every sentence to slow the rate of speech and sharpen word choice; occasionally pausing mid-sentence to break up monotonous rhythm and pull back wandering attention; and inserting longer, even awkward pauses after important points to let students process information and anticipate what comes next. He explains that these pauses not only improve retention and engagement but also give teachers a built-in moment to assess how well students are following along and adjust accordingly. The piece frames pausing as a foundational storytelling and instructional skill that makes teachers more interesting, their words more meaningful, and their classrooms more attentive.
points: Many teachers who struggle to hold attention are unknowingly talking too fast, stringing sentences together without breaks.
Pausing a beat between sentences slows speech, sharpens word choice, and curbs rambling.
Pausing mid-sentence breaks up monotonous rhythm and pulls back students whose attention has started to wander.
Longer, even awkward pauses after key points let students process information and anticipate what comes next.
Strategic pausing doubles as a built-in checkpoint for teachers to assess whether students are following along.
quotes: Do you ever get the feeling your students aren’t hearing a word you say?
One common denominator among those who struggle with getting students to listen is that they talk too fast.
Pausing, in fact, is one of the most important skills for capturing and keeping attention. It can also improve behavior, eliminate boredom, and make your instruction more interesting.
It breaks up the rhythm of your speech, which can quickly grow monotonous. It brings students back into the fold whose minds have started to wander.
It gives students a chance to download the information, reflect on it, and consider how it pertains to them.
A lengthy pause also adds drama and intrigue to even the most mundane topics. It's a critical element of effective storytelling and can help make your subject come alive for your students.
Instead of slouching down and away in their seats, they’ll lean toward you. Like a field of daisies reaching for the sun.
